title: Research Design
display_name: Research Design
abstract: Abstract This chapter describes the research design that this book develops and uses to test its arguments empirically and operationalizes key variables and alternative explanations to this account. It introduces the comparative-historical method whereby the following empirical chapters test different parts of the argument and provides an overview of its nested design which combines data at the individual, party-political, and (inter)national level analysed using both statistical methods and a comparative case study. It then presents the case selection, data, and operationalizations that are used across the book’s three empirical chapters, as well as how these account for key alternative explanations.

title: Introduction
display_name: Introduction
abstract: Abstract This chapter introduces the phenomenon of rising varieties of populism across democracies in recent decades and situates the book’s main arguments in the literature. It defines populism and discusses how it is seen and studied as a threat to democracy and the liberal international order (LIO) of recent decades in liberal political theory, comparative politics, and international relations, whereas others insist on the normative variety of different populisms beyond the radical right. Against this background, the chapter introduces the book’s main arguments which address how the LIO itself may have contributed to gains for varieties of populism due to self-undermining dynamics of inherently liberal international institutional features. It presents the empirical and theoretical scope conditions of this account and its contributions to the literature. The chapter ends with how the book is structured to develop and test its arguments and discuss its findings’ implications for the crises of liberal (international) order.

title: ‘The People’ vs. the LIO?
display_name: ‘The People’ vs. the LIO?
abstract: Abstract This chapter operationalizes and empirically studies how varieties of populism challenge liberal and democratic principles in the liberal international order (LIO). It first develops observable implications about how the mechanism of democratic legitimacy depletion may normatively vary across types of populism at the individual and party level to present either an authoritarian nationalist threat or a cosmopolitan democratic corrective. These expectations are then tested using survey data on citizens from up to thirty-seven liberal democracies between 1996 and 2017 as well as using case study evidence from populist party manifestos in an EU subsample. Results corroborate the key distinction between exclusionary and inclusionary types of populism including regarding international institutions. But they also provide further evidence that inclusionary populism on the radical left is disadvantaged to exploit democratic legitimacy depletion in the LIO, so that the rise of populism overall pushes the LIO more strongly towards nationalist authoritarianism rather than cosmopolitan democratization.

title: Political parties and participation: migrants’ subjective knowledge about their representatives
display_name: Political parties and participation: migrants’ subjective knowledge about their representatives
abstract: People's knowledge about their representatives is important because it informs about the quality of democracy and can predict future political behaviours. In spite of this, we know little about why migrants (do not) know who their representatives are. This article seeks to address this gap in the literature and explains the migrants’ subjective knowledge about parliamentarians. The study uses individual data from an original survey conducted in June-July 2022 among 1,058 Romanian migrants. The strongest predictors for knowledge are linked to political parties and participation, while the transnational ties and the intention to return have no effects.

title: When Do Broken Campaign Promises Matter? Evidence From Four Experiments
display_name: When Do Broken Campaign Promises Matter? Evidence From Four Experiments
abstract: Campaign promises are a central mechanism for voters to hold politicians accountable, and information about their breakage or fulfillment features prominently in the media during election campaigns. Despite the importance of campaign promises, previous research yields conflicting expectations regarding their influence on citizens. Some theories suggest citizens vote based on policy performance and, therefore, consistently penalize actors who break their promises. Other theoretical accounts, however, argue that exposure to information during election campaigns often has minimal effects on citizens due to strongly held prior beliefs and partisan motivations. The goal of the current study is to address these competing claims by systematically testing the conditions under which citizens penalize politicians for breaking promises. We conducted four experiments (total N = 7,030), three of them preregistered, in two countries under varying political conditions. We find that (1) broken promises decrease domain-specific evaluations of leaders but have little impact on evaluations of actors’ overall performance; (2) broken promises have limited effects when people have strong priors about the political actor who made the promise; and (3) citizens downplay and rationalize promises broken by ingroup, but not outgroup, leaders. These results suggest that even though information about broken promises is salient in campaign communications, its impact on citizens is context-dependent and often quite limited.

abstract: Resumo: Este artigo analisa as percepções de manifestantes que participaram dos protestos de junho de 2013. Através de entrevistas em profundidade, realizadas nos meses seguintes às manifestações, buscamos analisar as narrativas dos ativistas sobre os rituais de participação, suas percepções sobre a natureza e motivações dos protestos e o modo pelo qual foram atraídos ou convocados a participar das mobilizações. Apesar da diversidade de perfis e da grande quantidade de pautas emergentes durante os protestos, identificamos duas formas principais de constituição e participação dos sujeitos políticos, a partir da distinção entre indivíduos com e sem experiência política ou associativa prévia. Neste artigo, observamos como essas diferenças influenciaram as formas de participação e os diversos enquadramentos dos manifestantes em relação aos partidos e à representação política.

title: Polarization over the priority of political problems
display_name: Polarization over the priority of political problems
abstract: Abstract What drives ideological division about political problems? When prioritizing which problems are most in need of redress, voters might disagree about the severity of individual outcomes that constitute such problems; the prevalence of those problems; or whether such problems are amenable to solution by government action. We field a large survey experiment in the United Kingdom and the United States and develop a new measurement approach that allows us to evaluate how ideological disagreements change when respondents consider the individual badness, social severity, and priority for government action of a set of 41 political problems. We find that large ideological divergences are observed in beliefs about social severity and priority for government action, not individual problem badness, and only in the United States. An important implication of these results is that perceptions of problem prevalence are a key source of polarization over problem‐prioritization in the United States.

title: Incentives to Join a Local Party Association: Evidence from Canada
display_name: Incentives to Join a Local Party Association: Evidence from Canada
abstract: Abstract The comparative literature has devoted considerable attention to why individuals join political parties. This is especially important in the context of the declining party membership and activism that political parties face in contemporary politics. While the question of why members join parties has been well-documented, considerably less work has considered incentives to join other party positions. In the Canadian case, for example, we know very little about the incentives to join an electoral district association (EDA). This is surprising given the consequential role—both formal and informal—that local party associations and their presidents have been known to play in intra-party politics (influencing candidate nomination, membership recruitment and so forth). This study applies Clark and Wilson's (1961) framework of material, solidary and purposive incentives to local party association membership and asks why individuals join their local party executive and whether this motivation shapes the subsequent character of the EDA.

title: Understanding Public Support for Electoral Reform in Ontario, Canada
display_name: Understanding Public Support for Electoral Reform in Ontario, Canada
abstract: In recent years, activist groups across Canada have advocated for electoral reforms at all levels of government, including changes to the electoral system, opportunities to cast ballots online, a reduction in the minimum voting age, and an extension of the voting franchise to long-time residents who are noncitizens. At present, very little is known about public support for these reforms and how support varies by reform type and level of government. Drawing on a large survey of eligible voters in Ontario, we find that public opinion varies substantially across reforms, with high support for internet voting and ranked ballots, and lower support for changes to the franchise. We also find that support is stronger for reform at the municipal level than it is either provincially or federally. Finally, we find that partisanship is an important predictor of reform attitudes. We conclude with a discussion of the possible policy implications of our findings.

title: Partisan voters in party systems with ephemeral parties: Evidence from South Korea
display_name: Partisan voters in party systems with ephemeral parties: Evidence from South Korea
abstract: In this article, we examine how voters make decisions about electoral candidates in an under-institutionalized party system. In such a context, parties are expected to be less rooted in society, with fewer programmatic linkages to particular groups. Thus, voters are considered less likely to vote for candidates based on their policy positions and are expected to have less consistent policy preferences. Instead, it is assumed that individual candidate characteristics are more important. Using a conjoint survey experiment conducted in South Korea, a crucial case of a weak party system in a relatively new but consolidated democracy, we examine how voters are motivated by individual candidate characters and domestic policy and foreign policy positions. Our results show that individual characteristics matter, but we also find strong evidence of consistent policy preferences, especially in the foreign policy domain. We demonstrate high levels of programmatic partisanship – voters who are partisans informed about and primarily motivated by policy positions.

title: Who Gets Mobilized?
display_name: Who Gets Mobilized?
abstract: Abstract This chapter shifts the focus to relations between employers and their employees. It argues that employers who have more leverage over their employees are more likely to engage in workplace mobilization. In slack labor markets the threats and demands of employers will carry greater weight because it is harder for workers to find alternative employment. Survey data from Russia show that workplace mobilization is particularly common in single-company towns where voters have few exit options. We also argue that employees in the state sector who generally have fewer transportable skills and less attractive alternatives are more likely to be mobilized by their employers. Survey data from six countries show that workplace mobilization is far more common among public sector employees than in the private sector.

title: Introduction
display_name: Introduction
abstract: Abstract This chapter conceptualizes workplace mobilization as a form of clientelist political mobilization. When compared to party activists, employers have more leverage over voters and use more coercion. However, in contrast to party activists, their reach is limited to the workplace and mobilization by employers is disdained by most voters. These differences between party activists and employers constitute a starting point for investigating the central question in the book: why do employers mobilize their workers to vote? Employers are effective vote brokers because they sit atop preexisting hierarchies and have influence over large numbers of voters. This chapter introduces our core arguments about why and when workplace mobilization occurs and previews our main findings. It also discusses how the study of workplace mobilization contributes to the study of electoral subversion, autocracy, political economy, clientelism, and Russian politics.

title: What Is Workplace Mobilization?
display_name: What Is Workplace Mobilization?
abstract: Abstract This chapter defines workplace mobilization, reviews related studies, and introduces the data sources used throughout the book, including two surveys with firm managers; five individual surveys in Russia; surveys in Ukraine, Venezuela, Argentina, Indonesia, Nigeria, and Turkey; two focus groups and ten in-depth interviews in Russia; and a range of observational and qualitative data from Russia. Using these data, this chapter characterizes the scope and nature of workplace mobilization. The practice takes a variety of forms ranging from rallies, employer-provided transportation, agitation on the shop floor, to threats of dismissal and intimidation. Employers use both carrots and sticks to influence voter behavior, but the latter are much more common, which makes workplace mobilization unpopular. This chapter provides evidence that voters in a range of settings disapprove of the practice.

title: Why Do Employers Mobilize?
display_name: Why Do Employers Mobilize?
abstract: Abstract Few studies in political science examine workplace mobilization in depth and those that do tend to focus on relations between employers and workers. This chapter explores an equally important piece of the puzzle: relations between politicians and employers. Since the costs of workplace mobilization are real, employers often must receive incentives to mobilize their workers. This chapter argues that politicians can provide inducements—negative or positive, implicit or explicit—that incentivize employers to mobilize their workers. In Russia, the primary focus of this chapter, these inducements are typically provided by the state. This chapter provides empirical evidence that (1) employers perceive the costs of mobilization, (2) the state incentivizes employers to mobilize, and (3) employers respond to these incentives by mobilizing their employees. In this way, we conceive of workplace mobilization as a bargain struck between employers and politicians.

title: Who Mobilizes?
display_name: Who Mobilizes?
abstract: Abstract This chapter addresses why some firms mobilize their workers during elections, but others do not. It argues that workplace mobilization is especially likely where politicians exercise greater leverage over firm managers, and where, in turn, managers exercise greater leverage over their employees. This leverage often emanates from the availability of outside options for employers and employees. Data from firm surveys in Russia support these arguments. This chapter also finds that workplace mobilization occurs where the transaction costs between politicians and managers are lower. When politicians and managers have close personal or organizational ties, they are more likely to reach and abide by an agreement about how to share the costs and benefits of workplace mobilization. Thus, workplace mobilization not only is forged by relative power relations but also emanates from the nature of personal elite relationships.

title: Is Workplace Mobilization Effective?
display_name: Is Workplace Mobilization Effective?
abstract: Abstract This chapter examines why politicians choose to rely on employers to mobilize votes. Politicians prefer vote brokers who can mobilize large numbers of votes at relatively low cost. In many settings, employers’ leverage over employees gives them a powerful stick to influence whether and how their employees vote. This chapter combines focus group data, observational survey data, and framing experiments to argue that mobilization by employers increases voter turnout and therefore can help politicians win elections. Using survey data from a range of countries, we find that workplace mobilization is correlated with higher turnout in a range of settings. And using survey experiments in Russia and Venezuela, we find that the average voter is more likely to respond to turnout appeals from employers than they are to appeals from party activists.

title: Is Workplace Mobilization Undemocratic?
display_name: Is Workplace Mobilization Undemocratic?
abstract: Abstract This chapter identifies the conditions under which workplace mobilization should be seen as acceptable from the perspective of democratic theory. We argue that workplace mobilization can enhance democracy when it neither infringes on voter autonomy nor leads to systematic bias in electoral outcomes. These conditions are difficult to satisfy in practice. Employers often use threats to mobilize workers and target the most economically vulnerable among them. In addition, incumbents are far better positioned to engage in workplace mobilization than are challengers. The analysis in this chapter relies heavily on the experience of the United States—a country that has experienced periods where employers once applied coercive methods and more recent periods where such techniques have largely been replaced by more sophisticated tactics that require more nuanced normative judgments.

title: How Do Voters Respond?
display_name: How Do Voters Respond?
abstract: Abstract Using data from Russia and the United States, this chapter examines how the general voting public responds to workplace mobilization. The study finds that voters are willing to withdraw their support for candidates and parties that mobilize their workers, especially when the practice is coercive. Politicians who use employers as vote brokers face a trade-off: workplace mobilization can increase electoral support by getting workers inside the company to the polls, but doing so can reduce support among voters outside the company who disapprove of the practice. In contexts where media freedom is greater, voters are more likely to learn about workplace mobilization. In these information-rich settings, the gains to politicians from mobilizing workers can be outweighed by the reduction in support from voters who oppose the tactic. This chapter shows that workplace mobilization is indeed less prevalent in Russian regions with greater media freedom.

title: Implications and Next Steps
display_name: Implications and Next Steps
abstract: Abstract This chapter summarizes the book’s findings and discusses the implications of its analysis for political science. Workplace mobilization is an important and understudied form of clientelism. Its prevalence demonstrates that clientelism can persist in the modern world. The book also suggests an additional reason why economic and political liberalization so often go hand in hand. Economic liberalization increases the autonomy of company managers from the state and makes it harder for politicians to subvert elections by inducing employers to engage in workplace mobilization. The findings also generate new insights into economic theories of democratization, suggesting that asset specificity may undermine democracy because the holders of such assets are particularly vulnerable to pressures from politicians to mobilize their workers. The chapter concludes with a series of policy recommendations and some reflections on possible future research.

title: The Symbolic Organisation of Political Antagonism: An Integrative Model of Cultural and Social Polarisation
display_name: The Symbolic Organisation of Political Antagonism: An Integrative Model of Cultural and Social Polarisation
abstract: This article develops a cultural and relational model of political polarisation that integrates insights from currently disconnected streams of scholarship to conceive polarisation as a discursive and performative struggle over meaning. Rather than treating polarisation as mere attitudinal divergence, we frame it as the symbolic organization of political antagonism. Our model identifies three interrelated symbolic dimensions: divergence on contested issues conceptualized as signifiers; the consistency of these divergent issues, enabling chains of signification held together by “linking signifiers” that mark group identity; and the mutual constitution of opposing semiotic chains and identities. We add a fourth, social dimension by distinguishing symbolic from social boundaries and outline the various ways in which they interact. This framework offers a sociological theory of polarisation attentive to meaning-making, affect, boundary formation, co-constitution, and the conditional relationship between cultural and social differentiation.

title: The Covid-19 pandemic and its impact on political cleavages in Europe: Lessons learned and policy recommendations for democratic resilience
display_name: The Covid-19 pandemic and its impact on political cleavages in Europe: Lessons learned and policy recommendations for democratic resilience
abstract: The Covid-19 pandemic has profoundly impacted European political landscapes, not by creating entirely new cleavages but by activating, intensifying, and reconfiguring existing political divisions. This policy paper examines how the pandemic affected political cleavages across the European Union. The analysis reveals the emergence of a health-economy trade-off dimension, the differential activation of economic versus cultural grievances, and the strategic role of populist radical right parties (PRRPs) in politicizing the crisis. Key findings indicate that while the pandemic created new arenas of contestation, traditional ideological orientations and trust in scientific institutions remained the strongest predictors of political attitudes and behaviors. The paper concludes with a set of policy recommendations for managing future crises while maintaining democratic resilience and social cohesion.

title: Ethno-Regional Parties Cannot Be Everything to Everyone: Electoral Risks of a More Diverse Issue Agenda
display_name: Ethno-Regional Parties Cannot Be Everything to Everyone: Electoral Risks of a More Diverse Issue Agenda
abstract: This note suggests that should ethno-regional parties broaden their agenda, they could be electorally punished. Literature suggests an electoral incentive to a broader party issue agenda, even for some ‘niche’ parties. However as quintessential ‘niche’ parties due to their limited ability to be competitive with the general electorate, we argue ethno-regional parties can only gain votes by specializing on a narrow, concentrated set of issues. They will have limited success when engaging in broad or diverse issue competition with mainstream issues. Using over 40 years of electoral data from eight advanced capitalist democracies, our main empirical finding is that, as Ethno-regional parties broaden or diversify their issue agenda they are likely to lose subsequent vote share.

title: Existem Clivagens Políticas no Brasil?
display_name: Existem Clivagens Políticas no Brasil?
abstract: Resumo O artigo problematiza a existência de clivagens políticas no Brasil, quais os seus tipos e se elas conectam eleitores e partidos. Inicia-se com o debate teórico sobre os problemas da abordagem sobre clivagens de Lipset e Rokkan (1967) e as atualizações teóricas do campo. Para os testes empíricos, são utilizados dados de pesquisas de opinião com eleitores e com deputados, entre 1997 e 2023. Os resultados apontam para a existência de divisões estáveis no eleitorado, especialmente em torno da dimensão liberal-fundamentalista, que estão associadas tanto às características demográficas dos eleitores, quanto às suas preferências partidárias. Tais divisões, porém, conectam fracamente eleitores e partidos em termos de congruência política.

title: Policy proximity and candidate repositioning: The value of consistency
display_name: Policy proximity and candidate repositioning: The value of consistency
abstract: Candidates and parties often have to decide in campaigns whether to remain consistent on policy positions that do not match the median voter or reposition towards moderate. This type of strategic ‘flip-flopping’ is controversial and debated regularly in the media. This study provides causal evidence on this topic by placing candidates and voters on the same policy scale in an experimental setting (n = 4351). Candidates randomly reposition to the centre, extremes, or remain consistent on a non-median position. This creates a test of repositioning versus consistency within the framework of proximity voting. To precisely estimate proximity, the policy is operationalized as numbers: preferred number of asylum seekers resettled annually. Results show that consistent positioning caused a substantial increase in favorability among those who were proximally close. This suggests that consistency is especially important to voters who hold the same position as the candidate. Repositioning toward respondents’ position did not change favorability, but repositioning away from respondents caused a reduction in favorability. The strategically important median voter subgroup did not increase support for candidates who adopted their preferred position. Taken together, this suggests that consistently supporting a non-median immigration policy is preferred to repositioning to the middle.

title: Sorting It Out in the American States: Party Ideology and Mass Alignment
display_name: Sorting It Out in the American States: Party Ideology and Mass Alignment
abstract: Abstract While partisan cleavages in the United States are well documented, less is known about how the ideological positioning of state political parties shapes individual-level partisan sorting and issue alignment. This article examines whether citizens’ ideological and policy positions are influenced by the extremity of their own party and by the overall level of polarization between state parties. Using data from the Cooperative Election Study (2014–2020) merged with Shor–McCarty measures of state party ideology, we find that state party positioning matters for mass sorting. Individuals are more likely to align with their party’s issue stances when their own party is ideologically extreme, but greater polarization between state parties is associated with weaker issue alignment. These results highlight the asymmetric ways in which citizens respond to their partisan environments, demonstrating that state-level party positioning—not just national polarization—plays an independent role in shaping partisan sorting in the United States.

title: On Polarization and Partisan Attachments: Greater Consistency but not Greater Strength
display_name: On Polarization and Partisan Attachments: Greater Consistency but not Greater Strength
abstract: Abstract Are Americans more strongly attached to their political parties than ever before? Despite partisanship’s stronger associations across politics, inter-election panel surveys show that the durability of partisan attachments has slightly weakened. After bringing attention to this fact, I propose that this discrepancy exists because comparisons across time are mostly a product of greater consistency in mass partisan behavior, not the strengthening of mass partisan attachments. Model estimates confirm that thermometer- and vote-based indicators of partisanship have mostly become more consistent markers of partisanship instead of representing stronger modern-day partisan orientations. These estimates find that American partisan attachments have strengthened since the 1970s but remain similar to the 1950s and 1960s. American partisanship is clearly a more relevant and consistent conduit for mass political opinion and behavior in recent years, but American partisan attachments are not much stronger; they are just as movable now as they were in the past.

title: The Digital Spin: Political Agenda Setting on Alternative Social Media Platforms
display_name: The Digital Spin: Political Agenda Setting on Alternative Social Media Platforms
abstract: ABSTRACT Objective This study examines how agenda setting operates in today's hybrid media ecosystem by investigating how mainstream political events during the 2024 US election year were discussed on alternative social media platforms. Methods The study analyzes over 2000 mainstream news articles about high‐profile political events from January to March 2024, and related discourse across Facebook, Gab, Truth Social, and Telegram using Structural Topic Modeling and sentiment analysis. Results Alternative platforms create parallel information ecosystems that challenge traditional mechanisms of agenda setting. Three dominant topics emerged: Trump and election issues (40%), global conflict and US foreign policy (20%), and immigration (20%). These narratives exploit fear and anger with negative tones, but also incorporate humanizing language. Conclusions Alternative platforms construct parallel information ecosystems that rival traditional agenda‐setting mechanisms.

title: Making campaigns more personalised: Explaining the personalisation of election campaigns in comparative perspective
display_name: Making campaigns more personalised: Explaining the personalisation of election campaigns in comparative perspective
abstract: What factors are associated with the personalisation of election campaigns? Previous research on this subject suggests that individual and contextual factors contribute to fostering the personalisation of election campaigns. Building on prior studies, I argue that two significant trends in election campaigns worldwide – namely, professionalisation and the incorporation of social media for campaigning – correlate with more personalised campaigns. I test this hypothesis using data from the second wave of the Comparative Candidate Survey (CCS) and multilevel Bayesian models. Results indicate that candidates who intensively use social media are more likely to conduct personalised campaigns. Similarly, the involvement of professional consultants is also associated with an increase in the personalisation of election campaigns. These findings shed light on how recent transformations in the campaign environment and campaign organisation may affect the degree of personalisation in election campaigns. Overall, these findings contribute to a better understanding of the personalisation of election campaigns from a comparative perspective.

title: Neuroticism Is Linked With Liberal Ideology in Young, but not Old, People in the United States
display_name: Neuroticism Is Linked With Liberal Ideology in Young, but not Old, People in the United States
abstract: ABSTRACT Polarization in the United States is partly due to a remarkable ideological divide between generations. Although substantial research has investigated why old people have become more conservative, less is known about why young people have become more liberal. The article investigates this by probing the role of neuroticism. It hypothesises that, compared to older cohorts, younger ones have grown up during a more competitive historical period that has led many to become more neurotic and, in turn, to support the left. This predicts that, in the United States, neuroticism is linked with liberal ideology in young, but not old, people. This prediction is supported in two studies. A third study found no such effect outside the United States, suggesting that the effect observed in the United States is not due to aging but to generational experiences. Overall, these findings highlight a potential role for neuroticism in explaining why young Americans have become more liberal.

title: Building a Broken Wall: Small Cities, Nonpartisanship, and Polarization
display_name: Building a Broken Wall: Small Cities, Nonpartisanship, and Polarization
abstract: This is an accepted article with a DOI pre-assigned that is not yet published.Nonpartisanship has been a core element of U.S. local government for over a century. Today, these institutions face a new challenge as polarization has grown more intense, intimate, and ideological. Drawing on a detailed study of nonpartisan city councils across 14 small cities in Wisconsin in 2020 and 2021, this paper examines how these institutions have confronted the contemporary moment of partisan conflict. First, by analyzing council member backgrounds, meeting minutes, and voting patterns, this paper finds that the administrative practices of nonpartisanship—adopted in the era of urban machine politics—fail to constrain partisan polarization. Second, by conducting a qualitative analysis of video recordings of city council meetings, this paper documents important cultural conflict over the meaning of nonpartisanship. The cultural struggle over nonpartisanship both allows nonpartisanship to remain an organizing force in local government and provides new opportunities for partisan conflict and division. The paper concludes that this situation—where cultural practices of nonpartisanship dominate as administrative practices weaken—causes new challenges for the practice of local government, local policymaking, and the potential for nonpartisanship to counterbalance polarization.

title: Sharing Prime Ministerial Power in Hung Parliamentary Systems: Deputy, Rotating and Alternating Prime Ministers
display_name: Sharing Prime Ministerial Power in Hung Parliamentary Systems: Deputy, Rotating and Alternating Prime Ministers
abstract: In parliamentary systems without clear coalition formation paths, prime ministerial powers become key to power-sharing between coalition partners. Coalition formateurs strategically use deputy, rotating, and alternating prime minister arrangements to build coalitions. Using coalition theory and examples from parliamentary systems, this study examines these strategies, focusing on Israel as a case study where all of these arrangements have been tested. The research shows that hung parliaments and increased presidentialization of the prime minister’s office lead to more pronounced power-sharing of prime ministerial functions. While this strategy enables coalition formation in difficult circumstances, it does not guarantee coalition stability.

title: Party Types in the Age of Personalized Politics
display_name: Party Types in the Age of Personalized Politics
abstract: Democracies in general and political parties in particular have undergone political personalization in recent decades. The power balance between politicians (one or many) and the team (the party as a collegial entity) has changed, and existing party typologies are no longer suited to the analysis of today’s democratic politics. Although some new personalized party types have been added, what is missing is a systematic attempt to contrast them with the collegial option. This article proposes a new classiﬁcation of political parties to ﬁll the lacuna. It includes ﬁve ideal types of parties: two personalized-decentralized types, referring to collections of separated autonomous activists or to separated autonomous individual politicians (plural); a collegial type, which is about the centrality of the team and is based mainly on collective authorities and collective decision making; and two personalized-centralized types, referring to the centrality of an individual politician in her capacity as the party leader or that of a speciﬁc individual who “owns” the party.

title: Leaders or parties? Practices of candidate selection in Western Europe
display_name: Leaders or parties? Practices of candidate selection in Western Europe
abstract: Political parties still play a fundamental gatekeeping role in selecting candidates and, consequently, in selecting parliamentary and governmental elites. Nonetheless, the effective room for maneuver of party leaders in candidate selection has not received much attention. This is an interesting area to investigate, also considering recent accounts of intra-party personalization of politics, where party leaders have allegedly become more central. By using a novel dataset on approximately 75 Western European parties and some 250 party leaders between the mid-1980s and the mid-2010s, this article analyzes party leaders’ autonomy in selecting candidates for general elections. It tests the effect of party leaders’ determinants (e.g., leadership tenure or leaders' gender) and party determinants (i.e., party membership). Both leader-related and party-related determinants have a significant impact. The results show that political parties can still act as a counterbalancing force vis-à-vis party leaders and call for further investigation into intra-party informal practices.

title: Parasites, Colluders, and Adversaries: Explaining Mafia Strategies Toward Public Institutions in Italy
display_name: Parasites, Colluders, and Adversaries: Explaining Mafia Strategies Toward Public Institutions in Italy
abstract: Organized crime groups use coercion, corruption, and collusion with political actors to achieve their aims. Why do organized crime organizations sometimes quietly coexist with local authorities, sometimes collude with them, and at other times threaten or attack them? Once restricted to few areas in advanced democracies, recent literature and media attention have shown how the impact of organized crime on political arenas is spreading across new and old democracies. This article examines how local political and economic conditions shape the strategies that organized crime adopts toward public institutions. We propose a typology of three main strategies—parasitic, collusive, and adversarial—and explore the conditions under which each emerges. Using an original data set covering almost 8000 Italian municipalities, we show that collusion is most likely where weak political parties leave local political systems open to infiltration, while adversarial strategies arise where high levels of public spending make control over resources especially valuable. The analysis demonstrates that criminal behavior is not random but responds to identifiable political and economic incentives. Beyond the Italian case, these findings illuminate how variations in democratic institutions and local economies can foster different forms of organized crime behavior.

title: Closer to the people: the impact of politicians’ working-class affiliation on their ability to evoke feelings of symbolic representation among the general population and the working class
display_name: Closer to the people: the impact of politicians’ working-class affiliation on their ability to evoke feelings of symbolic representation among the general population and the working class
abstract: Abstract A central tenet of democracy is “government of the people, by the people, for the people”, implying that representatives should reflect the citizens they serve. However, ethnic minorities, young people, women, and the working class are often underrepresented in legislatures. Previous literature suggests that increasing representation of these groups can address this bias, both by advancing their interests in policymaking and by providing symbolic value by signaling more inclusive government. To examine whether working-class politicians evoke stronger feelings of symbolic representation, particularly among the working class, I conduct a factorial survey experiment in Germany, in which 1,033 respondents rate five hypothetical political candidates with differing social and political profiles. The results indicate that people favor politicians from modest backgrounds and perceive them to be better representatives of citizens’ interests, more accessible, and more trustworthy. This effect is particularly prominent among respondents self-identifying as working class.

title: Measuring the effects of differentially intense information on political opinions
display_name: Measuring the effects of differentially intense information on political opinions
abstract: The field of public opinion has already extensively addressed how political opinions form and change. However, we still need to find out why some information flows affect opinions more effectively than others. The concept of intensity is employed to assess the differential penetrating power attributed to different political information flows. A measure of the intensity of information flows is presented and tested on British respondents with a survey experiment that employs vignettes with information flows concerning the former British Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May. This study finds that the measure of intensity is able to identify information flows that have a larger probability of affecting opinions. Information flows characterised by higher intensity are more likely than information flows characterised by low intensity to influence opinion formation about the former British leader. Still, respondents' pre-existing political awareness and predispositions condition the effect of information flow intensity in agreement with established theories in public opinion. Different political awareness and predispositions are associated with different reactions to the intensity of information flows. Finally, the study finds that effects can be observed only if the information flow is intense enough, independent of the respondents' attitudes.

title: Presidential approval, party brands, and candidate quality in U.S. national elections
display_name: Presidential approval, party brands, and candidate quality in U.S. national elections
abstract: This article considers (1) presidential approval, (2) party brand differentials, as measured by the generic ballot, and (3) the presidential candidate polling differentials during the general election campaign to forecast the 2024 U.S. presidential and congressional elections. While all these three mass public opinion variables are leveraged to forecast collective partisan election outcomes, we consider the variables together as theoretically distinct determinants of partisan fortunes at both the executive and legislative levels and make the following contributions. First, using novel time-series data of mass opinion since 1937, we show that all three variables are weakly correlated and thus distinct conceptual and empirical measures of mass public assessments of partisan stimuli. Second, we use these three mass opinion variables to specify a unified model of U.S. national elections which better predicts variation in electoral outcomes compared to the standard forecasting approaches, finding that congressional election outcomes are predicted by party brands while presidential elections are predicted by presidential approval and the presidential candidate polling differentials heading into election day. Lastly, we validate our forecasting model using out-of-sample and 2024 forecasting predictions against other standard forecasting approaches.

title: The Partito Democratico in Italy
display_name: The Partito Democratico in Italy
abstract: Abstract This chapter argues that the Democratic Party of Italy has securitized immigration by actively translating from the Right the tropes that some Muslim immigrants might be ‘radicals’ and ultimately a problem for national security. The Democratic Party has securitized by flagging liberal-progressive and left-wing referent objects, such as human security and gender equality. This linguistic choice is missed by both Copenhagen and Paris Schools since both would focus on the Italian government as a de-politicized actor, without questioning party ideologies. The chapter interprets the securitization of the Mediterranean refugee crisis as a significant example of active translation from the Italian Right to the Democratic Party. In the Italian context, talking about Islam means talking about immigration, as recent flows came mostly from Muslim-majority countries and since 1.5 million of the 2.7 million Muslims in Italy are foreign citizens. The Democratic Party has translated by balancing between border policing and the respect of human security. This ambivalence is old wine in a new bottle. The Italian centre-left parties securitized immigration long before the recent immigration ‘crisis’, at least since the management of immigration flows from Albania in the 1990s and Libya in the following decade. The author then explains that the Democratic Party securitized Islam by using references to gender equality. Finally, the author shows that translation led some Democratic Party factions to contest the governance of Mediterranean immigration supported by the executive and to propose a more inclusive reform of the Italian citizenship regime (based on ius sanguinis).

title: Translation
display_name: Translation
abstract: Abstract This chapter explains the meaning and dimensions of translation. It argues that translation is active, collective, and contextual and that parties craft securitization through a circular movement of collision, appropriation, and reformulation of words. Through this process, parties interact as both agents and audiences involved into the translation of securitization and in its rejection, which can lead to the de-securitization of an issue. The author explains firstly that parties translate actively. The purpose is to avoid passive imitation and to present the final product as better than the original. Although the appropriation of other parties’ tropes is used to appeal to larger electorates, it mainly seeps into the ideological repertoire of each party to keep its traditional values, norms, and identities consistent and show coherence in front of internal and external audiences. Then, the author explains that translation is a collective process. Although it can be spearheaded by individual party leaders, it is effectively achieved by internal factions and by a cluster of mediators that work behind the stage. Party leaders, factions, and mediators work to translate alternative ideological baggage into their vocabulary. Internal factionalism matters for translation and has been even strengthened in the context of the growing personalization of politics. If factions do not express sufficient convergence of interests, translations might fail and de-securitization might follow suit. Finally, the author reflects on how translations within and across parties occur in the sociocultural context where they are made and read. The translations across parties are nested in a distal context marked by left-wing orientalist and Islamophobic legacies, and in the proximate context of party interaction across the political spectrum.

title: Islamophobia and Translations of Securitization in the UK, France, and Italy
display_name: Islamophobia and Translations of Securitization in the UK, France, and Italy
abstract: Abstract This book contributes to research on Islamophobia and critical security studies by exploring the historical trajectory and the intra-party dynamics that led three Western European centre-left parties (British Labour Party, French Socialist Party, and Italian Democratic Party) to securitize Islam. Western governments have increasingly framed Islam as a threat to national security in recent decades. Yet, the ideas and languages through which securitization manifests across and inside right-wing and left-wing parties is less examined by current literature. This book shows that political parties translate security (particularly the securitization of Islam) in the name of various ideological references. This is necessary to understand why the same securitized threat (Muslims) is interpreted differently by political parties on the Right and the Left. The author engages with one main question: How do Islamophobia and specifically its securitarian dimension travel across and inside political parties? The author argues that the securitization of Islam travels across and inside parties through a process called translation, which occurs through the appropriation of tropes traditionally belonging to the other political pole. Translation is active, because Islamophobic tropes are translated into a language coherent with partisan ideologies. Translation is also collective. If the securitization audiences are not persuaded by translation, the process might be rejected, and such rejection can lead to de-securitization. Translation is also influenced and made possible by contextual elements: the party history, the interaction between the Right and the Left, and significant external events that increased the perception of insecurity raised by Muslims.

title: The British Labour Party
display_name: The British Labour Party
abstract: Abstract This chapter argues that the British Labour Party has securitized Muslims in the name of ‘balanced race relations’. This securitization has happened through two translations: one involves the right-wing meaning of security, translated as ‘law and order’ instead of more left-leaning connotations (e.g. security as fight against socio-economic marginalization); the other involves the trope about Islam as a cultural and demographic concern for British society. Translation is grounded in Labour’s historical ambivalence towards immigration and is influenced by authoritarian and populist tropes coming from British right-wing parties (e.g. the Conservatives, UKIP, British National Party). The chapter takes issue with the Copenhagen School of securitization because this approach would consider securitization only as an ‘exceptional’ move above and beyond politics. The author challenges this view and integrates it through a close engagement with party mutual appropriation of Islamophobic tropes. In doing so, the author shows that the securitization of Muslims under New Labour’s governments was not the mere consequence of critical junctures such as the 7 July 2005 London bombings, despite their understandable emotional impact. Translation depended on distal and proximate contexts, in which Labour developed a substantial ambiguity between promotion of multiculturalism and suspicion towards Black and Brown minorities. In the end, the chapter reflects on the collective nature of translation by analysing Labour’s internal reactions to the War on Terror and counterterrorism policies like Prevent. Contextualized within the internal feuds between Labour’s Right and Left, the author explains that former Labour leader Corbyn advanced an alternative agenda to de-securitize Muslims and revise the British counterterrorism strategy.

title: Conclusion
display_name: Conclusion
abstract: Abstract The conclusion highlights that the puzzle and arguments advanced in the book carry much significance in light of the electoral growth of radical right parties in Britain (Reform UK), France (National Rally), and Italy (Brothers of Italy). It reiterates the importance of the notion of translation to grasp how Islamophobia and its securitarian dimensions travel across countries and parties. Exploring this process allows moving beyond the methodological state-centrism of Copenhagen and Paris Schools of securitization and enriching Critical Security Studies through a focus on political parties. Then, it explains the added value of a comparative approach to elicit affinities and differences in the way Islamophobic tropes travel across the Right and Left in the three countries under scrutiny. Finally, it recalls the normative implications of the debates about securitizing Islam and discloses promising areas for further investigation in the study of Islamophobia among European political parties.

title: The Travel of Islamophobia Across the Right and the Left
display_name: The Travel of Islamophobia Across the Right and the Left
abstract: Abstract This chapter argues that Western European right-wing and left-wing parties have appropriated each other’s Islamophobic tropes to better justify the securitization of Islam to their electors. It aims at explaining the context in which the travel of four specific tropes across conservative/right-wing and liberal-progressive/left-wing ideologies occurred. This context is marked by what the author defines as ‘critical junctures’, namely, moments of urgency when the feeling of insecurity towards political Islam rapidly escalated, such as the Rushdie and Creil affairs in 1989, the hundreds of victims in the jihadist terrorist attacks committed by Al-Qaeda and ISIL, as well as Brexit and the Mediterranean refugee crisis of 2015. The four Islamophobic tropes discussed in the chapter are: ‘Islam is a different civilization that violently clashes with the West’; ‘Muslim immigration is a demographic threat’; ‘Islam is incapable of separating the political sphere from the religious sphere’; ‘Islam is a patriarchal religion that poses obstacles to gender equality’. The first and second tropes sit comfortably with right-wing conservative ideologies, the third and the fourth tropes with liberal-progressive and left-leaning one. Such a wide range of stereotyped views on Muslims provides the ideological background behind current forms of securitization of Islam. The chapter then engages with securitization theories, arguing that the Copenhagen and Paris Schools do not provide the right framework to understand why the same threat (Islam) is securitized in different ways by parties of various political ideologies. To decipher this dynamic, the author proposes engaging with the concept of translation, which explains how securitization moves inside and outside parties.

title: The Parti Socialiste in France
display_name: The Parti Socialiste in France
abstract: Abstract This chapter argues that the French Socialist Party (Parti Socialiste) has translated the securitization of Islam in the name of referent objects understandable to its electors. Amongst its referent objects, laïcité (the constitutional principle of secularism in France) gained prominent importance during the Hollande presidency in the context of the jihadist terrorist attacks committed in 2012 and 2015. Rather than interpreting the Socialists’ counterterrorism agenda only as an emergency reaction to jihadism, the author shows that securitization was part of routinized discussions already animated in the party by engaging with the Paris School, whose authors rightly claim that securitization is normal rather than exceptional. However, they underplay the partisan debates that drive translation and shape the way securitization is articulated. Instead, the Socialist securitization has happened through a translation from the Right of securitarian and Islamophobic tropes. Translation was nested into specific distal and proximate contexts. This move was intelligible to left-wing audiences because laïcité is part of the history of the French Left, and was already used to securitize Muslims in the 1980s (for instance in the Creil affair of 1989). The Socialists further securitized Muslims in the name of secularism after two conjunctures: first, the translation of a conservative connotation of security by important cadres of the party between the 1990s and 2000s; second, the translation of laïcité by right-wing parties, such as the National Rally, which have appropriated it as an instrument to discriminate against Muslims. The chapter concludes by discussing how the reactionary discourse on security and Islam fractured the party. It raised much furore among the internal left-wing factions, who called to reject the securitization of Islam.

title: Introduction
display_name: Introduction
abstract: Abstract This chapter introduces the central puzzle of the book, namely, how Islamophobic narratives and policies are translated across right-wing and left-wing parties in Britain, France, and Italy. It situates my inquiry within existing debates in critical studies on security, comparative politics, and research on Islam in Europe. While this body of scholarship has reflected on why Islam has become a top security threat for Western governments, little has been said on how political parties of different ideologies translate it in their own vocabulary. The chapter foregrounds the notion of translation and outlines the theoretical framework (securitization theory) that guides my analysis. It also fleshes out my methodological approach, based on interpretivism and critical discourse analysis, and discusses some important normative concerns. Finally, the introduction presents the book’s overall structure, helping the reader to navigate the subsequent chapters. In doing so, it establishes a foundation for the arguments developed in the pages ahead.

title: The Authoritarian Belief System
display_name: The Authoritarian Belief System
abstract: Abstract Chapter 4 documents the emergence of a broader “authoritarian belief system” in the White public. It demonstrates that authoritarianism now constrains a wide range of sociocultural attitudes. Moral traditionalism, racial conservatism, hostility to immigration, concern for social order, and defense attitudes are (as of 2020) tightly correlated with one another and with authoritarianism among White Americans. Analyses covering the 1992–2020 period indicate that authoritarianism-based attitude consistency increased considerably from 1992 to 2020 among White Americans. The chapter also shows that authoritarianism-based attitude consistency is greater among college-educated White respondents in all periods, but that it has increased more among non-college Whites. Importantly, it finds pronounced effects of the 2016 and 2020 elections on authoritarianism-based constraint among both college and non-college Whites, reinforcing the argument that elections in which sociocultural divisions are salient—such as the 2016 and 2020 Trump elections—can increase the impact of the authoritarian predisposition.

title: Treating a friend to voter registration in a Divided America
display_name: Treating a friend to voter registration in a Divided America
abstract: As partisanship strengthens in the United States, unaffiliated voter registration is also increasing. We conducted an original survey experiment to understand voter registration choices among registered voters in Florida and North Carolina, two states with substantial shares of unaffiliated registrants and persistent partisan polarization, but with differing primary participation rules. Institutionally, Florida holds closed primaries where only those registered with a political party may participate in the respective primary for that party. North Carolina holds semi-closed primaries that allow those not registered with a political party (i.e., unaffiliated registrants) to vote in party primary elections. The results of our experiment demonstrate that institutional context matters. Specifically, informing respondents of primary participation rules shapes voter registration recommendations. Among registrants who identify as independents, exposure to Florida's closed primary rule causes them to be more likely to recommend party registration, whereas awareness of the semi-closed North Carolina primary rule makes independents and partisans more likely to advise unaffiliated registration. However, in the absence of information explaining rules for primary participation, respondents are more likely to suggest that their friend register in alignment with their own political identity. In summary, our study provides valuable insights into how registration choices are conditioned by political identities and exposure to treatments that emphasize political conditions and primary participation rules.

title: President Obama's Victories in Illinois: 2012 Compared to 2008
display_name: President Obama's Victories in Illinois: 2012 Compared to 2008
abstract: This paper describes and analyzes President Obama’s 2012 election victory in Illinois and compares it to his earlier victory in 2008 in his home state. It also extends the analysis back through the 2004 and 2000 presidential elections and shows how those results were similar and where they differed. It primarily relies on the county and county election returns supplemented by U. S. Census data as the unit of analysis. The paper sets Illinois into a national electoral context describing what is happening in an era of deep partisan polarization coupled with the prospects for a partisan realignment.

title: Partisan-Colored Glasses? How Polarization has Affected the Formation and Impact of Party Competence Evaluations
display_name: Partisan-Colored Glasses? How Polarization has Affected the Formation and Impact of Party Competence Evaluations
abstract: The potential effects of mass polarization has become a major subject of study in political science. Multiple studies have shown that polarization at the mass level has caused political attitudes and opinions to be increasingly driven by party identification over the past few decades. Even responses to questions as nonpartisan as “Has the economy gotten better or worse over the past year?” show a partisan bias (Bartels 2002). In this paper, I look at whether party identification is having an increasing impact on party competence evaluations, as would be expected if polarization has happened at the mass level. I first study whether the effect of party identification on vote choice in House and Senate elections from 1986 through 2012 has increased, or whether the growing power of party identification is being filtered through party competence evaluations, causing the effect of these evaluations on vote choice to increase. I then look at the direct effect of party identification on party competence evaluations to see if the effect of party identification on competence evaluations has grown between 1986 and 2012, and if the effect of retrospective economic evaluations on competence evaluations has decreased at the same time. Results show that there is no clear trend in the effect of party competence evaluations and party identification on vote choice over time. However, the effect of party identification on competence evaluations has clearly risen between 1986 and 2012.

title: The Diversity of Latino Ideology
display_name: The Diversity of Latino Ideology
abstract: Ideology in American politics is usually measured along a liberal-conservative continuum depending on a person’s position on issues such as the role of government in the economy and the regulation of social behavior. This framework has been a poor fit for understanding Latino political behavior. This dissertation argues that to understand Latino political behavior it is necessary to understand Latinos’ ideological thinking. I argue that Latinos’ shared cultural traits and their core beliefs (rooted in a common experience) inform three distinct Ethno-Ideologies: pan-ethnic, co-ethnic and ethnic. These Ethno-Ideologies sort Latinos depending on how much in common they think share with other Latinos. To test the theory, I use data from the 2006 Latino National Survey, the largest nationally-representative survey of Latinos. These data are supplemented with qualitative insights from focus groups conducted with Latinos in Phoenix, Arizona. The findings suggest that ideological thinking among Latinos in the U.S. is more rooted in the experience in which the core beliefs are based than in their shared cultural traits.

title: Social Policy and Social Services in Women's Pregnancy Decision-Making: Political and Programmatic Implications
display_name: Social Policy and Social Services in Women's Pregnancy Decision-Making: Political and Programmatic Implications
abstract: This dissertation empirically evaluates the argument that welfare state expansion will reduce abortion. Its central question concerns the extent to which women's economic needs and the degree to which social services meet them influence their abortion decisions. It also investigates the characteristics and political behavior of pro-life, pro-social welfare Americans, the most likely targets of any effort to reframe welfare as a pro-life issue. To these ends, this project employs individual-level data from the National Election Study, the Fragile Families Study, and a survey of clients at Baltimore abortion providers and pregnancy centers. Other main data sources include state welfare policies and abortion rates, and neighborhood-level Census data linked to directories of child care and abortion providers. This project represents perhaps the first rigorous, social-scientific investigation of the link between economic assistance and abortion decisions. Its findings contribute to the literature on policy compliance and policy tools, and carry implications for social welfare politics and the composition of party coalitions. In many ways, data analyzed in this study align with the status quo of abortion and welfare policy and politics. Political debates over welfare are largely independent of political debates over abortion. Likewise, the cases in which the root issues associated with low-income women's abortion decisions could be exclusively solved by welfare policy are rare. Welfare policy appears to be an effective capacity-building tool with respect to abortion decisions for some women, in some ways, and in combination with other supports. The pro-life movement's current dominant approach to abortion policy appears to meet the movement's goal of reducing abortions more efficiently than a capacity-building approach. Investment in capacity-building policy or in political messages of that tone holds promise for progress toward their respective policy and political goals. On the other hand, expected gain is modest considering both of these efforts would stretch the limits of the possible in American politics.

title: „My i oni” – granice symboliczne klasy średniej w Polsce
display_name: „My i oni” – granice symboliczne klasy średniej w Polsce
abstract: Granice symboliczne to pojęcia-linie obejmujące niektórych ludzi i rzeczy, podczas gdy inni zostają wykluczeni. Badacze i badaczki dowodzą, że podziały my/oni są produktem pracy nad granicami i w dużej mierze zależą od znaczeń, jakie ludzie im nadają. Istotną rolę w tym procesie odgrywają zarówno repertuary kulturowe, do których mogą się odwołać, jak i strukturalne warunki, w jakich żyją. Celem artykułu jest odpowiedź na pytanie dotyczące mechanizmów konstruowania granic symbolicznych przez osoby należące do klasy średniej w Polsce. Jakie kategorie i schematy klasyfikacyjne stosują, aby określić różnice między ludźmi takimi jak „my” a ludźmi takimi jak „oni”, oraz jakie strategie argumentacyjne wykorzystują do podtrzymywania i legitymizowania tych podziałów? Analiza indywidualnych wywiadów pogłębionych wskazała na istnienie wewnętrznych różnic w obrębie klasy średniej (frakcja ekonomiczna/frakcja kulturowa) oraz wpływ kontekstu społecznego na to, w jaki sposób badani z Warszawy i Wałbrzycha konstruują granice symboliczne swojej klasy.

title: The Political and Psychological Dynamics of Authoritarianism
display_name: The Political and Psychological Dynamics of Authoritarianism
abstract: Abstract Chapter 2 develops a theoretical account of how and for whom authoritarianism has restructured American political life. First, it observes that authoritarianism has more strongly influenced preferences among White Americans than other racial and ethnic groups, especially when it comes to voting and partisanship. Second, it argues that among White Americans many of the sociocultural issues that have grown salient in recent decades reflect a common influence of authoritarianism and the emergence of an increasingly constrained authoritarian belief system. Third, it argues that White Americans have come to differ more in voting and partisanship as a function of authoritarianism, but that this sorting process has been contingent on the salience of sociocultural division between the parties and on education. It also predicts that authoritarianism will shape perceptions of partisan polarization and citizen closeness to the parties. Finally, it argues that authoritarianism should now predict attitudes toward democracy itself.

title: Authoritarianism and Its Consequences in an Ideologically Divided Party System
display_name: Authoritarianism and Its Consequences in an Ideologically Divided Party System
abstract: Abstract Chapter 8 examines how changes in the images of the parties relate to authoritarianism-based sorting of White Americans. First, it shows that White Americans at all authoritarianism levels came to see the parties as more ideologically different from 1992 to 2020. Second, it finds that authoritarianism is more strongly associated with Republican presidential voting among White Americans who see a larger ideological gap between the two parties. Third, it shows that White Americans came to see themselves as more ideologically distant from the party that is least aligned with their level of authoritarianism from 1992 to 2020 (i.e., the Democratic Party for authoritarian Whites, the GOP for nonauthoritarian Whites). Finally, it demonstrates that White authoritarians and nonauthoritarians show a growing tendency to tolerate ideological mismatch, voting for the candidate whose party’s sociocultural branding best matches their level of authoritarianism even when the opposition candidate is seen as ideologically closer.

title: Authoritarianism and Antidemocratic Attitudes in the Trump Era
display_name: Authoritarianism and Antidemocratic Attitudes in the Trump Era
abstract: Abstract Chapter 9 examines the relationship between authoritarianism and support for democracy among White Americans who form the majority of the US electorate. Using recent observational data, it shows that authoritarianism predicts antidemocratic attitudes among Whites regardless of partisanship, though White Republicans have become uniformly cooler to democracy. It supplements this analysis with a survey experiment that manipulated a conservative candidate’s commitment to democracy. Despite the greater polarization of White partisans on both authoritarianism and commitment to democracy, we found that conservative candidates who made explicitly antidemocratic appeals were slightly less attractive to both White authoritarians and nonauthoritarians. Adding an antidemocratic appeal did not boost the appeal of conservative candidates—even conservative candidates that “tempted” White authoritarians with a promise to reduce immigration. That said, we also find that the most authoritarian Whites show more support than others for conservative candidates even when the latter explicitly reject democracy in counter-normative ways.

title: Authoritarianism and the Future of American Democracy
display_name: Authoritarianism and the Future of American Democracy
abstract: Abstract Chapter 10 recaps the volume’s findings and their contributions to the literature, and discusses the limitations of the analysis. It also elaborates on what the findings mean for the trajectory of American democracy in coming years. First, it discusses the implications of the findings for the cohesiveness of the two US party coalitions. Second, it asks whether the growing overlap between authoritarianism and partisanship may weaken uniform commitment to democracy across the partisan divide. Ultimately, it returns to the observation that authoritarian sorting is contingent to emphasize that authoritarianism is potentially dangerous to democracy only when competing party elites create an environment that leads citizens to sort on the basis of authoritarianism, when elites from the party that authoritarians have sorted into signal a willingness to degrade democracy, and when leaders fail to emphasize that social change and diversification can coexist with a sense of shared values.

title: Authoritarianism and Sociocultural Issue Defection
display_name: Authoritarianism and Sociocultural Issue Defection
abstract: Abstract Chapter 7 provides experimental evidence for a key argument about the contingent nature of authoritarian sorting among White Americans. It presents two experiments that demonstrate that ideological defection on sociocultural issues but not economic issues—that is, Republican candidates taking socially liberal positions or Democrats taking socially conservative positions—reduces the link between authoritarianism and Republican vote preference. Experiment 1 examines the moderating effect of issue defection to conservative positions by Democratic candidates. Experiment 2 examines the moderating effect of issue defection to liberal positions by Republican candidates. Both experiments find evidence for a strong “default” relationship between authoritarianism and Republican candidate preference in control conditions that present only biographical and party information. Treatments where a Democrat took a conservative position or a Republican took a liberal position eliminated this baseline relationship, but only when defection occurred on sociocultural (versus economic) issues.

title: The Authoritarian Tide
display_name: The Authoritarian Tide
abstract: Abstract This introductory chapter sets the stage for the theoretical and empirical analysis provided in the remaining chapters of the book. After describing the contemporary context of Trump-era US politics and describing the book’s research questions, it briefly reviews classic and contemporary research on authoritarianism. It introduces the argument that makes up the core contribution of the book: that attitudinal and partisan sorting as a function of authoritarianism among White Americans has played an important part in this story that needs to be comprehensively explored and, more importantly, that this sorting has been far more conditional and uneven over time than previous research on authoritarianism and public opinion has suggested. The book contends that authoritarianism has become foundational to understanding how polarization has unfolded in different segments of the American electorate over the last few decades. It concludes by providing an overview of the remaining chapters of the book.

title: Assessing Authoritarianism in the American Public
display_name: Assessing Authoritarianism in the American Public
abstract: Abstract Chapter 3 justifies the measurement strategy used. Following the work of other researchers, it operationalizes authoritarianism in terms of childrearing values. It shows that the four items that make up the measure are indicators of a single, temporally stable dimension among White Americans, and that it is highly correlated with other measures of authoritarianism. Importantly, it finds no evidence that political variables measured in 2016—partisanship, vote choice, and attitudes toward parties and candidates—had any significant relationship with change in authoritarianism from 2016 to 2020. This is critical to the ability to use authoritarianism as an exogenous predictor of changes in preferences in the White electorate. Finally, it shows that overall levels of authoritarianism among White Americans have remained very stable over the past three decades. Apparent changes in the character of American politics over these years thus cannot be a result of increasing absolute levels of authoritarianism among White Americans.

title: The Contingent Trajectory of Authoritarian Sorting Among White Americans
display_name: The Contingent Trajectory of Authoritarian Sorting Among White Americans
abstract: Abstract Chapter 5 uses 1992–2020 time-series data from the American National Election Studies to demonstrate that the relationship between authoritarianism and voting and partisanship has grown in an uneven fashion, increasing more notably when the parties offer candidates whose style and sociocultural appeals activate authoritarianism more strongly (e.g., the Trump elections in 2016 and 2020) but stalling or receding when the agenda turns away from sociocultural matters or the parties field candidates who are less distinct in their style and sociocultural orientation. Paralleling what was demonstrated for the authoritarian belief system in Chapter 4, it also shows authoritarian sorting among White survey respondents differs as a function of education, with stronger links between authoritarianism and voting and partisanship across time but much stronger increases in sorting among less-educated White respondents. Lastly, it shows that authoritarianism’s relationship with voting has become increasingly indirect and channeled through party identification over time.

title: Authoritarianism and the Mechanisms of Partisan Sorting
display_name: Authoritarianism and the Mechanisms of Partisan Sorting
abstract: Abstract Chapter 6 extends the volume’s analysis by looking at individual-level sorting among authoritarian and nonauthoritarian White respondents. This chapter zeroes in on the most intense periods of authoritarian sorting among Whites identified in Chapter 5—in 2004 and the lead-up to the Trump elections of 2016 and 2020. Individual-level results from multiple panel studies supplement the aggregate-level findings reported in the previous chapter. Over time, White voters are more likely to shift their partisan identification and patterns of voting when the latter conflict with their underlying level of authoritarianism. Interestingly, the results suggest that authoritarianism-based sorting has been asymmetric, with authoritarian White Democrats deserting their party more than nonauthoritarian Republican Whites have deserted theirs. Moreover, the 2016 and 2020 Trump elections had an especially strong effect on partisan identification: though the link between authoritarianism and voting remained stable from 2016–2020, the link between authoritarianism and party identification continued to grow.
